profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the platform team and the developer productivity team at a SaaS company preparing an internal rollout of a new AI-assisted coding workflow. The company is introducing a sidebar assistant inside the IDE plus a Slack-based chatbot for engineering questions, and the two workstreams need to align before a pilot starts next Monday. The immediate context is that the platform team owns the IDE integration and telemetry hooks, while the developer productivity team owns onboarding guidance, usage reporting, and the comparison deck for leadership about human-to-human versus human-to-bot support patterns in software engineering. The agenda is to confirm what will be shipped in the pilot, what data each side will hand off, how 'conversation' events will be counted in reporting, and who updates the shared rollout checklist and bot behavior notes. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on interfaces, handoffs, and reporting cadence for the pilot, even though several second-order assumptions remain misaligned.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: Engineering enablement, developer workflow analytics, onboarding programs, internal tooling adoption
members.background: Priya previously led rollout programs for code search and CI observability tools at two mid-sized engineering organizations and now runs developer enablement for the company's 500-engineer product org.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to look organized and lightweight for developers, avoid manual cleanup work for her team, and produce a clean leadership narrative about how AI chat changes support interactions without requiring a large instrumentation redesign.
hidden_assumptions: A 'conversation' should be counted as one developer help-seeking session, even if it spans several turns inside the same tool within a work block.
The pilot dashboard can rely on daily aggregated telemetry because leadership mainly needs adoption trends and broad comparisons, not event-level traces.
The shared rollout checklist is an enablement artifact owned by her team once engineering teams confirm technical readiness.
The 'bot notes' for the pilot means the short guidance page shown to developers about when to ask the chatbot versus another engineer, not the underlying system prompt or retrieval configuration.

members.name: Lucas Meyer
members.expertise: IDE extensions, service integration, event schemas, internal developer platforms
members.background: Lucas has spent the last four years building internal plugins and gateway services that connect third-party developer tools to company systems, and he is responsible for the new assistant's event pipeline and rollout package.
members.private_state: He wants to minimize risk during the pilot, preserve precise telemetry for debugging, and keep ownership boundaries clear so his team is not blamed for adoption materials or bot behavior after launch.
hidden_assumptions: A 'conversation' is a thread or session object emitted by the client integration, so each tool-specific session boundary should be preserved exactly as logged.
A handoff of telemetry means near-real-time event-level exports into the analytics bucket so anomalies can be traced back quickly during pilot week.
The shared rollout checklist remains owned by the technical integration team until all launch gates are closed because it is part of the release package.
The 'bot notes' are the actual assistant configuration notes and prompt/retrieval restrictions that the platform team maintains alongside the deployment.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to report 'conversation volume' for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means one developer help-seeking session, potentially combining multiple back-and-forth turns in the IDE assistant during a single task block and treated as one comparable unit against a human Slack exchange.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means one client-emitted session/thread object per tool, where a new sidebar session or Slack bot thread is a separate conversation regardless of user intent continuity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both work in adjacent tooling contexts where 'conversation' is a familiar and sensible term, and because they are coordinating reporting rather than debating research methodology, the surface agreement feels routine.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Lucas will send Priya the telemetry feed by end of day Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a daily aggregated table or dashboard-ready extract with counts by team, tool, and conversation category, suitable for leadership reporting and onboarding check-ins.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to expose raw near-real-time event exports in the analytics bucket, assuming Priya's analysts will derive whatever summaries they need.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software coordination meetings, 'send the telemetry feed' sounds sufficiently concrete because both sides are used to data handoffs, but each defaults to the artifact format common in their own function.

misalignment_points.topic: Ownership of the shared rollout checklist
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to keep the shared rollout checklist updated as teams finish their items.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes her enablement team owns the living checklist after technical readiness is confirmed, including onboarding, office hours, comms, and reporting tasks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes his platform team owns the checklist until pilot launch because it is part of the deployment readiness packet, and other teams merely fill in their rows.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe checklist maintenance has already been implicitly settled by prior launch habits, so neither thinks ownership needs to be restated in a short coordination call.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the latest 'bot notes' should be linked in the pilot packet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the developer-facing guidance note describing when to use the IDE assistant, when to ask the Slack bot, and when human-to-human escalation is better.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the internal technical notes covering prompt constraints, disabled commands, retrieval sources, and guardrail changes for the deployed bot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are plausibly called 'bot notes' inside the organization, both are relevant to rollout, and linking 'the latest one' sounds like a harmless administrative detail rather than a scope question.
